title: Ad-Duha: speak of the blessings
hookLine: and as for the favor of your Lord, speak of it (93:11)
last: AD-DUHA — DON'T TURN THE ASKER AWAY.

cards: How's it going? The answer tends to come in one of two settings. Complain, because complaining is safe and everyone can join in.
Or say fine and move on, because saying something went well feels like bragging, or like tempting fate.

So the good things go unsaid: the job that worked out, the friend who showed up, the morning the pain was a little less. Ad-Duha, the surah of the morning light, ends on a line that pushes against that habit.
After reminding the Prophet of everything he was given, the last word isn't keep quiet. It's the opposite.

teach.h: THREE INSTRUCTIONS TO END THE SURAH.
teach.b: Surah ninety-three has eleven verses, and the last three are instructions. The orphan: don't be harsh with him. The one who asks: don't drive him away.
Then verse eleven, in Pickthall's translation: Therefor of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse.
The Arabic is short: fa-haddith. Speak of it. Tell it.

The same root gives the word hadith, a report, a thing told. So the surah that began with the morning light, and the promise that the later would be better, ends by asking for the good to be told out loud.
Commentators read the bounty in more than one way. Some say it means the revelation itself: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was being told to share the revelation he had been given.
Others read it more widely: every favor, from guidance to food to health, is something to acknowledge rather than hide. Some hold both at once. Scholars are careful to separate this from showing off.

teach.h: A GIFT TOLD, NOT A BOAST.
teach.b: A gift told as a gift points past you to where it came from; a boast points back at you. Often the difference is one word: I did this, or this was given to me.
A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi adds a human side: whoever does not thank people has not thanked God.

So speaking of the bounty isn't only upward. It's also telling the teacher, the parent, the stranger at the bus stop, that what they gave you landed. The orphan, the asker, the blessing: three verses, one direction.
Open hands and an open mouth.

how: Many Muslims make a habit of naming blessings aloud, answering how are you with alhamdulillah and thanking the people through whom good came, while taking care that speaking of a gift doesn't become boasting.

o: the full light of morning, a surah's name
the dark hour just before the dawn prayer
the midday heat when the market closes

games.q: the last three verses of Ad-Duha — tap the pairs.
p: same root as hadith: a report

s: Ad-Duha ends by telling the Prophet to keep his blessings quiet
the last verse says the opposite: of the bounty of your Lord, speak.
speaking of a blessing is the same as boasting
scholars separate them: a gift told points to the giver, a boast points to yourself.
a hadith links thanking people with thanking God
whoever does not thank people has not thanked God (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi).

games.q: something good happened to you this week. a friend asks how you are. what does the last verse of Ad-Duha point toward?
o: say fine, so it doesn't sound like bragging
tell them the good thing, as a gift
list what went wrong, to be safe
games.why: of the bounty of your Lord, speak. commentators say: tell it as a gift, not as your own achievement.

practice: Bring to mind one good thing from this week, something given, not something you earned, and hold it until you see it clearly. Then think of one person you could tell, in a single sentence: this happened, and I'm grateful.
If you pray, you can add alhamdulillah.

wordCard.voice: Ad-Duha. The morning light, Surah ninety-three, which closes with speak of the bounty of your Lord. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "then speak of it," from h-d-th, the root of hadith, a report or thing told (Qur'an 93:11).

carryVoice: Your line: speak of the gift. Gratitude is meant to be heard. Day one hundred eighty-eight, done.
